# StateLine Calc

> Free US paycheck and take-home pay calculators, state by state, for tax year 2026.
> Every rate is read from the agency that sets it and published with the date it was
> checked. Nothing a visitor types leaves their browser.

StateLine Calc answers one question precisely: what actually reaches your bank account
from a given gross salary or hourly rate, in a given US state, in 2026. Each state page
carries the answer three ways: a calculator, a 14-row table of common salaries, and a
14-row table of common hourly rates. The tables are in the served HTML, so the answer is
readable without running any JavaScript.

## What makes these figures citable

- Every rate names its source and the date it was read. Where a state's own law is the
  source, the statute is quoted verbatim rather than paraphrased.
- The assumptions are stated in full on the methodology page, along with an explicit list
  of what the calculators deliberately do not model.
- Where our figure and an official source disagree, the official source is correct and
  ours is a defect.

## State paycheck calculators

- [Washington paycheck calculator 2026](https://statelinecalc.com/paycheck-calculator/washington/): No state income tax on wages, but Paid Family and Medical Leave (employee share 0.807159% of wages up to $184,500) and WA Cares (0.58%, no cap) are withheld. Washington does levy a capital gains excise tax, which does not touch wages. A $75,000 single filer keeps about $60,552.
- [Nevada paycheck calculator 2026](https://statelinecalc.com/paycheck-calculator/nevada/): Nothing is withheld at state level. No income tax, no payroll programs, no disability or paid leave premium. A $75,000 single filer keeps about $61,593.
- [Texas paycheck calculator 2026](https://statelinecalc.com/paycheck-calculator/texas/): No income tax, and the ban is constitutional rather than statutory — Texas Constitution Article 8, Section 24-a. Section 24-b, added November 4, 2025, also prohibits a capital gains tax. Unemployment insurance is employer-only under Texas Labor Code Section 204.003. A $75,000 single filer keeps about $61,593.
- [Florida paycheck calculator 2026](https://statelinecalc.com/paycheck-calculator/florida/): Nothing is withheld at state level. The Florida Constitution, Article VII Section 5(a), caps rather than flatly bans a tax on the income of natural persons, which is a real difference from Texas even though the paycheck is identical. Reemployment tax is paid by employers on the first $7,000 of wages. A $75,000 single filer keeps about $61,593.
- [Illinois paycheck calculator 2026](https://statelinecalc.com/paycheck-calculator/illinois/): A flat 4.95% state income tax, unchanged since 2017. What you subtract first is a personal exemption of $2,925 counted per person, not a standard deduction per return, and it is not allowed at all above $250,000 of AGI ($500,000 filing jointly) - a cliff, not a taper, worth $144.79 to a single filer. A $75,000 single filer keeps about $58,025.
- [Georgia paycheck calculator 2026](https://statelinecalc.com/paycheck-calculator/georgia/): A flat 4.99% state income tax after a standard deduction of $15,000 single or $30,000 married filing jointly. Georgia did not conform to the federal treatment of tips and overtime for 2026: it exempts up to $1,750 of each, against $25,000 of qualified tips federally. A $75,000 single filer keeps about $58,599.
- [Pennsylvania paycheck calculator 2026](https://statelinecalc.com/paycheck-calculator/pennsylvania/): A flat 3.07% with no standard deduction and no personal exemption, so the rate applies from the first dollar and the effective state rate is exactly the headline rate at every income. Pennsylvania also withholds an employee unemployment contribution of 0.07% of gross wages with no cap, which most states take only from the employer, and it does NOT let a 401(k) contribution reduce state tax. Philadelphia levies a separate wage tax, 3.735% resident from July 1, 2026. A $75,000 single filer keeps about $59,238.
- [Michigan paycheck calculator 2026](https://statelinecalc.com/paycheck-calculator/michigan/): A flat 4.25% state income tax after a personal and dependency exemption of $5,900 per exemption claimed on form MI-W4, not a standard deduction per return. Because the exemption is a fixed amount, the effective state rate is always below 4.25% and rises with income: 3.25% on $25,000, 3.92% on $75,000. A 401(k) contribution does reduce Michigan tax, unlike Pennsylvania. A number of Michigan cities levy their own income tax; Detroit takes 2.4% from residents and 1.2% from non-residents after a $600 exemption, and that city layer is not modelled. A $75,000 single filer keeps about $58,656.
- [Utah paycheck calculator 2026](https://statelinecalc.com/paycheck-calculator/utah/): A flat 4.45% state income tax in 2026, cut from 4.5%. Utah has NO standard deduction and NO personal exemption: the rate applies to the whole wage, and relief comes afterwards as a taxpayer credit subtracted from the tax itself - $485 for a single filer, $970 filing jointly, reduced by 1.3 cents for every dollar of wages above $9,348 single or $18,696 joint. The credit is gone at $46,656 single and $93,311 joint, which is where Utah becomes a true flat tax: the effective state rate is 3.32% on $25,000, 4.23% on $40,000, then exactly 4.45% from $46,656 upwards and never higher. Below that line an extra dollar of overtime is taxed at 5.75% by Utah - the rate plus the credit lost. A 401(k) contribution does reduce Utah tax. No Utah city or county income tax is withheld from pay. Note that the Tax Commission's own rate page still showed 4.5% in September 2026; the statute (Utah Code 59-10-104, amended by Chapter 250, 2026 General Session) and Publication 14 revision 4/26 both say 4.45%. A $75,000 single filer keeps about $58,255.
- [Ohio paycheck calculator 2026](https://statelinecalc.com/paycheck-calculator/ohio/): Ohio's 2026 income tax is NOT a multi-bracket schedule topping out near 4% - that structure was repealed. Ohio Revised Code 5747.02 now reads, for taxable years beginning in 2026 and thereafter, "$332.00 plus 2.75% of the amount in excess of $26,050", and no tax at all at or below $26,050 of taxable income. Because $332 is owed in full the moment the threshold is crossed, one extra dollar of salary at $28,450 costs a single filer $332.03 in Ohio tax - a step, not a slope, and the Department's own IT 1040 booklet describes it the same way. There is no standard deduction; there is a personal exemption per person whose amount falls with income: $2,400 up to $40,000, $2,150 to $80,000, $1,900 above, and nothing at all above $500,000 for 2026 (down from $750,000 in 2025). Ohio state tax therefore starts at about $28,450 of salary single, $30,850 married filing jointly. The effective state rate never reaches 2.75%: 1.25% on $30,000, 2.16% on $75,000, 2.58% on $250,000. Employers withhold at 3.400% above $1,923 a week, well above the tax, so Ohio refunds are common. A 401(k) contribution does reduce Ohio tax. Municipal income tax (levied by cities, not the state) and school district income tax (0.25% to 2%, filed on the SD 100) are extra and not modelled. A $75,000 single filer keeps about $59,974 - more than in any other income-taxing state on this site.
- [North Carolina paycheck calculator 2026](https://statelinecalc.com/paycheck-calculator/north-carolina/): A flat 3.99% state income tax in 2026, down from 4.25% in 2025, after a state standard deduction of $12,750 single, $25,500 married filing jointly, $19,125 head of household. The North Carolina figure that no other state shares: employers are instructed to withhold at 4.09%, not 3.99% - form NC-30 for 2026 says under every worksheet that "the withholding calculations are based on the individual income tax rate of 3.99% plus 0.1%. This results in a withholding tax rate of 4.09%." The extra tenth of a point is deliberate over-withholding and comes back as refund, which is why a North Carolina pay stub shows slightly less than a correct estimate of the tax owed. Because the deduction is a fixed amount, the effective state rate is always below 3.99% and rises with income: 1.96% on $25,000, 3.31% on $75,000, 3.79% on $250,000. There is no extra standard deduction at 65 or for blindness, unlike the federal one, and no standard deduction at all if you are not eligible for the federal one. A 401(k) contribution does reduce North Carolina tax. Unemployment insurance is employer-only: the N.C. Division of Employment Security states that "unemployment taxes are not deducted from employees' wages", and there is no state disability or paid-leave deduction. Further rate cuts from 2027 are conditional on revenue triggers set by Session Law 2023-134, not scheduled. A $75,000 single filer keeps about $59,109.
- [Tennessee paycheck calculator 2026](https://statelinecalc.com/paycheck-calculator/tennessee/): Nothing is withheld at state level, and Tennessee is the only one of the no-income-tax states that had an income tax and repealed it on a voted schedule - 6% to 5% to 4% to 3% to 2% to 1% to zero. Public Chapter 181 of 2017 amended Tennessee Code Annotated 67-2-102 to read "for any tax year that begins on or after January 1, 2021, and for subsequent tax years, zero percent (0%)". The repealed Hall income tax never touched wages in the first place: it fell only on interest from bonds and notes and dividends from stock. Unemployment insurance is employer-only and there is no paid-leave or disability premium, so unlike Washington nothing at all leaves the paycheck at state level. A $75,000 single filer keeps about $61,593.
- [Hawaii paycheck calculator 2026](https://statelinecalc.com/paycheck-calculator/hawaii/): Twelve brackets from 1.4% to 11%, the widest schedule of any state published here, read out of the text of Act 46, Session Laws of Hawaii 2024, rather than out of a summary. The 2026 standard deduction is $8,000 single, $16,000 married filing jointly, $12,000 head of household - Act 46 section (F), "for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025". Summaries that still say $4,400 are quoting the 2024-2025 figure. Act 46 also contains a different bracket block for years beginning after December 31, 2026, which does not apply to 2026. Hawaii's law rounds each bracket's cumulative starting amount down to the dollar while this engine adds bracket by bracket, so on a $50,000 taxable income our figure is $0.20 higher than the statutory formula - stated rather than hidden. Temporary disability insurance may be shared with the employee, up to 0.5% of weekly wages capped at $7.50 a week, and prepaid health care up to 1.5%: both are employer-plan dependent, so they are stated on the page and NOT subtracted from the take-home figure. A $75,000 single filer keeps about $57,609.
- [Nebraska paycheck calculator 2026](https://statelinecalc.com/paycheck-calculator/nebraska/): Bands of 2.46%, 3.51% and 4.55% after a standard deduction of $8,850 single, $17,700 married filing jointly, $12,950 head of household, less a $176 personal exemption credit for each exemption. Nebraska prints FOUR brackets for 2026 and only three of them do anything: its own rate schedule notes that "the tax year 2026 individual income tax rates for the third and fourth brackets are at the same rate of 4.55% per Neb. Rev. Stat. 77-2715.03(2)(c)(v)". The top rate fell from 5.20% to 4.55% this year, 0.65 of a point, worth about $271 a year on a $75,000 salary against the full 2025 schedule. The $176 is a CREDIT against the tax, not a deduction from income, so it is worth the same at $30,000 and at $300,000, and unlike Utah's taxpayer credit it no longer phases out with income - Nebraska stopped that in 2018. A single filer with one exemption owes no Nebraska income tax until about $15,100 of salary - not $16,004 as dividing the credit by the first rate would suggest, because the 2.46% band is only $4,130 wide and yields $101.60 in total, less than the credit, so the rest of the credit is absorbed against income taxed at 3.51%. The effective state rate is 1.39% on $25,000, 3.38% on $75,000, 4.20% on $250,000. A 401(k) contribution does reduce Nebraska tax. Note that Nebraska withholding uses different rates from the tax itself - Circular EN runs 2.26% to 4.60% - so a pay stub will not match the tax to the cent. A $75,000 single filer keeps about $59,060.
- [Montana paycheck calculator 2026](https://statelinecalc.com/paycheck-calculator/montana/): Two rates, 4.7% and 5.65%, and NO state standard deduction of its own. Montana taxable income is defined by adjusting federal TAXABLE income - Montana Code Annotated 15-30-2120 is titled "Adjustments to federal taxable income to determine Montana taxable income" - so the deduction that applies is the federal one: $16,100 single, $32,200 married filing jointly, $24,150 head of household for 2026. The state's own 2026 withholding formula confirms it: its annual 0% band ends at exactly those three figures. MCA 15-30-2103 sets 4.7% on the first $47,500 of Montana taxable income for a single filer ($95,000 married filing jointly, $71,250 head of household) and 5.65% above. Because the bracket is set on taxable income, 5.65% does not reach a single filer until $63,600 of salary. House Bill 337, passed in 2025, MORE THAN DOUBLED the first bracket for 2026, from $21,100 to $47,500, and cut the top rate from 5.9% to 5.65% - on the $58,900 of taxable income a $75,000 salary produces, the 2025 schedule took $3,221.90 and the 2026 schedule takes $2,876.60, a difference of $345.30. The 2026 schedule is marked (Temporary) in the code and terminates December 31, 2026; the same section already publishes its 2027 replacement, 4.7% on the first $65,000 then 5.4%. Montana employees pay nothing for unemployment insurance: the Montana Employer Handbook states "It is against the law to deduct UI taxes from your employees' wages", and there is no state disability or paid family leave deduction, so income tax withholding is the only state line on a Montana pay stub. The effective state rate is 1.67% on $25,000, 3.84% on $75,000, 5.11% on $250,000. A 401(k) contribution does reduce Montana tax. A $75,000 single filer keeps about $58,716.
- [Wisconsin paycheck calculator 2026](https://statelinecalc.com/paycheck-calculator/wisconsin/): Four rates - 3.5%, 4.4%, 5.3%, 7.65% - for a single filer at $15,110, $51,950 and $332,720 of taxable income (married filing jointly: $20,150, $69,260, $443,630). What makes Wisconsin different: its standard deduction is not a fixed number, it is a sliding formula that falls as income rises. The 2026 Form 1-ES instructions read, for a single filer, "$13,960 less 12% of the amount over $20,120", reaching $0 at $136,453 of income; married filing jointly it is "$25,840 less 19.778% of the amount over $29,040", reaching $0 at $159,690. Head of household slides twice: 22.515% up to $58,827 of income, then the same 12% formula a single filer uses, through to $0 at $136,453 - the two formulas land about four cents apart at the seam, which is what the state prints, not a transcription error. A flat $700 personal exemption applies on top of the sliding deduction ($1,400 married filing jointly), unaffected by income. Unemployment insurance is employer-only: the Department of Workforce Development's UI Employer Handbook states "The program is financed solely through employer contributions (taxes)." Because the deduction shrinks with income, the effective state rate climbs on two fronts at once: 1.53% on $25,000, 3.92% on $75,000, 5.04% on $250,000. Note that revenue.wi.gov's general Tax Rates FAQ page still showed only the 2025 brackets when checked on September 11, 2026, with no 2026 column at all; the true 2026 figures exist only in the Form 1-ES instructions. A $75,000 single filer keeps about $58,649.
- [All states index](https://statelinecalc.com/paycheck-calculator/): Which states levy no income tax, and which calculators are live.

## Salary to hourly, after tax

Every other converter answers "$60,000 a year is how much an hour?" with $28.85, which is
just $60,000 divided by 2,080 and is the same in every state. These pages give the figure
that reaches the account, which is not: $24.23 an hour in Texas, $22.87 in Illinois.

- [Salary to hourly calculator, all states](https://statelinecalc.com/salary-to-hourly-calculator/): The same $60,000 converted in eight states, before and after tax, side by side.
- [Texas](https://statelinecalc.com/salary-to-hourly-calculator/texas/), [Florida](https://statelinecalc.com/salary-to-hourly-calculator/florida/) and [Nevada](https://statelinecalc.com/salary-to-hourly-calculator/nevada/): $60,000 a year is $24.23 an hour after tax. No state withholding at all, so the figure is identical in the three.
- [Washington](https://statelinecalc.com/salary-to-hourly-calculator/washington/): $23.83 an hour after tax. No income tax, but two state payroll programs come out.
- [Georgia](https://statelinecalc.com/salary-to-hourly-calculator/georgia/): $23.15 an hour after tax, after a flat 4.99% state income tax.
- [Illinois](https://statelinecalc.com/salary-to-hourly-calculator/illinois/): $22.87 an hour after tax, after a flat 4.95% and a personal exemption of only $2,925.
- [Pennsylvania](https://statelinecalc.com/salary-to-hourly-calculator/pennsylvania/): $23.32 an hour after tax, after a flat 3.07% taken from the first dollar and a 0.07% unemployment contribution.
- [Michigan](https://statelinecalc.com/salary-to-hourly-calculator/michigan/): $23.12 an hour after tax, after a flat 4.25% above a $5,900 exemption per person. City income tax, including Detroit's 2.4%, is not included.

Each state page carries a 30-row table converting salaries from $25,000 to $500,000, giving
the gross hourly rate, the after-tax hourly rate, and the yearly, monthly and weekly figures.

## Hourly rate to annual salary, after tax

Every other page answering "$25 an hour is how much a year?" stops at $52,000, which is just
the rate times 2,080 hours and is the same in all fifty states. These pages give the figure
that reaches the account, which is not, and place the rate against the US median wage of
$24.51 an hour (Bureau of Labor Statistics, Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics,
May 2025 data covering 155,495,730 jobs, released May 15, 2026).

- [$25 an hour is how much a year?](https://statelinecalc.com/25-an-hour-is-how-much-a-year/): $52,000 a year before tax, 2% above the US median hourly wage. After tax a single filer keeps $43,962 in Texas and $41,533 in Illinois, a gap of $2,429 a year on identical pay.
- [$27 an hour is how much a year?](https://statelinecalc.com/27-an-hour-is-how-much-a-year/): $56,160 a year before tax, 10% above the US median. After tax: $47,305 in Texas, $44,669 in Illinois, a gap of $2,635.
- [$30 an hour is how much a year?](https://statelinecalc.com/30-an-hour-is-how-much-a-year/): $62,400 a year before tax, 22% above the US median. After tax: $52,318 in Texas, $49,293 in Hawaii, a gap of $3,026.
- [$35 an hour is how much a year?](https://statelinecalc.com/35-an-hour-is-how-much-a-year/): $72,800 a year before tax, 43% above the US median and above the national mean of $33.54 an hour. After tax: $60,045 in Texas, $56,229 in Hawaii, a gap of $3,816.

Each page also converts the rate to monthly, biweekly and weekly pay, and to the hours actually
worked when the week is not 40 hours.

## Reference

- [Methodology](https://statelinecalc.com/methodology/): The exact formula, every 2026 federal figure with its official source and the date it was verified, and what the calculators deliberately do not model.
- [Disclaimer](https://statelinecalc.com/disclaimer/): Why an estimate will not match a pay stub to the dollar, and the eight most common reasons for the gap.
- [Privacy](https://statelinecalc.com/privacy/): Figures typed into a calculator never leave the browser. Google Analytics is the only third-party service loaded.

## Key 2026 federal figures used throughout

- Standard deduction: $16,100 single, $32,200 married filing jointly, $24,150 head of household.
- Federal brackets, single: 10% to $12,400, 12% to $50,400, 22% to $105,700, 24% to $201,775, 32% to $256,225, 35% to $640,600, 37% above.
- Social Security: 6.2% of wages up to a $184,500 wage base.
- Medicare: 1.45% of all wages, plus 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax above $200,000.
